```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::knit_hooks$set(small_mar = function(before, options, envir) {
  if (before) par(mar = c(3.4, 3.4, 0.6, 0.6), mgp = c(2.1, 0.6, 0))
})
knitr::opts_chunk$set(small_mar = TRUE)

bbs <- read.csv("../data/BBS/FL_BBS.csv")
bobwhite <- bbs[bbs$Scientific_Name == "Colinus virginianus", ]
set.seed(2026)

power_design <- function(n_routes, n_years, decline = 0.03, mu0 = 10.8,
                         size = 1.15, nsim = 500) {
  mean(replicate(nsim, {
    yr <- rep(0:(n_years - 1), each = n_routes)
    cnt <- rnbinom(length(yr), mu = mu0 * (1 - decline)^yr, size = size)
    m <- lm(log(cnt + 1) ~ yr)
    summary(m)$coefficients["yr", "Pr(>|t|)"] < 0.05 && coef(m)["yr"] < 0
  }))
}
```

## The problem {.center}

## Meet the Northern Bobwhite {.smaller}

::: {.column width="52%"}
- A ground-nesting quail of **pine savanna, old fields and field edges**
- Lives in coveys, eats seeds and insects, named for its whistled call
- One of the **most hunted game birds** in the southeast
- Needs open, frequently burned understory

. . .

Fire suppression, denser pine plantations and intensive agriculture have taken

:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Thirty seconds of natural history, so the numbers later are about an animal
rather than a column.

Male and female in the photo: the male has the bold white throat and eyebrow
stripe, the female the buff version.

Why it is a good monitoring example: it is economically important, so somebody
will actually pay for the survey, and it is strongly tied to a habitat that
management can change, so the monitoring could inform a decision. That is the
difference between a survey and a science project.

Anyone who has spent time in longleaf pine country has probably heard one, even
if they have not seen one.
:::

## Northern Bobwhite are disappearing

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.1
#| fig-width: 6.4
yr <- aggregate(total_sightings ~ Year, data = bobwhite, FUN = mean)
plot(yr$Year, yr$total_sightings, pch = 16, col = "grey25",
     xlab = "year", ylab = "mean count per route")
abline(lm(total_sightings ~ Year, data = yr), col = "red", lwd = 3)
```

Florida Breeding Bird Survey, 1996 to 2019: about **3% fewer each year**.

::: {.notes}
Real data, the same BBS file from the last two lectures, and a real conservation
problem. Northern Bobwhite has declined across its range and is a species of
management concern in Florida.

A 3% annual decline compounds: that is roughly a halving in 23 years.

This decline took 24 years of survey data across dozens of routes to establish
confidently. That is the fact the rest of the lecture is about.
:::

## Your job

A state agency wants to monitor bobwhite on managed land.

They can fund about **400 route-visits** in total.

. . .

**How should they spend them?**

- Many routes for a few years?
- Few routes for many years?
- Something in between?

. . .

You will choose, and then we will find out who was right.

::: {.notes}
Set this up as a real decision with a fixed budget, because that is what makes it
a design problem rather than an arithmetic problem. A route-visit is one route
surveyed in one year, so 40 routes for 10 years and 20 routes for 20 years cost
the same.

Tell them the vote is coming. Knowing that a commitment is required changes how
they listen to the next few slides.
:::

## What is power? {.center}

## Four outcomes

| | $H_0$ is true | $H_0$ is false |
|---|---|---|
| **Reject $H_0$** | false positive, $\alpha$ | correct, **power** |
| **Do not reject** | correct, $1 - \alpha$ | miss, $\beta$ |

. . .

**Power = the probability of detecting an effect that is really there.**

Here: the chance the monitoring program finds the decline, given that bobwhite
really are declining.

::: {.notes}
The table is worth drawing slowly. Alpha is the one everybody knows, 0.05, and
it is about the world where nothing is happening. Power is about the world where
something is.

Most studies control alpha carefully and never think about power at all, which
is how fields end up full of underpowered studies that cannot settle anything.

Power is only defined once you say how big an effect you care about, which is
the point from Tuesday.
:::

## Power in a broader sense

Rather than fixating on p-values, ask:

- How does the **amount** of data change my answer?
- How does the **quality** of the data change my answer?
- How do I trade cost against what I can learn?

. . .

Other things worth simulating: **bias**, **precision**, **confidence interval
width**, **coverage**.

::: {.notes}
Power is the famous one, but the same simulation gives all of these, and some are
more useful. If the question is "how precisely could we estimate the rate of
decline", then CI width is the answer, not power.

Coverage is a good diagnostic for a method: simulate 1000 datasets, build a 95%
interval each time, and check that about 95% of them contain the true value. If
they do not, the method is broken.

This slide is also a menu for the final project for anyone who wants to go
further than the midterm.
:::

## Building the simulation {.center}

## Three things to decide

To simulate a monitoring program we have to say:

1. **How does the population change over time?** The deterministic part.
2. **How do counts vary around that?** The distribution.
3. **What numbers go in?** The parameters.

. . .

None of this is guesswork. The BBS data can answer all three.

::: {.notes}
Same three decisions as Tuesday, now on a real problem. Say that they are being
made deliberately rather than assumed, because the whole answer depends on them.

If any of the three is badly wrong, the power estimate is worthless. That is the
honest limitation of every power analysis, and it is why using real data for the
parameters matters.
:::

## 1. What shape is a decline? {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="47%"}
**Linear: lose the same number**

$$\mu_t = \mu_0 - c\,t$$

Reasonable if the loss is driven by something outside the population: a fixed
area of habitat cleared each year.

Reaches zero, then goes negative.
:::

::: {.column width="47%"}
**Exponential: lose the same fraction**

$$\mu_t = \mu_0\,(1 - d)^{\,t}$$

Reasonable if births and deaths scale with how many birds there are, which is
how populations usually work.

Approaches zero, never crosses it.
:::

::::

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.4
#| fig-width: 6.6
t <- 0:30
plot(t, 10.8 - 0.324 * t, type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "grey50", ylim = c(0, 12),
     xlab = "years from now", ylab = "expected count per route")
lines(t, 10.8 * 0.97^t, lwd = 3, col = "red")
abline(h = 0, lty = 3)
legend("topright", lwd = 3, col = c("grey50", "red"), bty = "n", cex = 0.9,
       legend = c("linear, c = 0.32", "exponential, d = 0.03"))
```

::: {.notes}
Both curves start at the same place and lose the same amount in year one, by
construction: 3% of 10.8 is 0.32. They end up in very different places.

We take the exponential, for the reason in the right column: a population of 10
birds cannot keep losing 0.32 birds a year forever. The same argument is why
population biology is written in rates rather than numbers.

Worth saying that the linear version is not silly. If the driver is habitat
being cleared at a fixed rate, losing a constant number is the better model, and
over a short window the two are nearly identical anyway, which the figure shows
for the first few years.

This is the multiplicative idea from Lecture 12, the one that makes things
lognormal, showing up here as a process rather than a distribution.

In R: `mu0 - c * t` and `mu0 * (1 - d)^t`.
:::

## Which shape does the data support? {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.7
#| fig-width: 6.6
ymeans <- aggregate(total_sightings ~ Year, data = bobwhite, FUN = mean)
ymeans$t <- ymeans$Year - min(ymeans$Year)
lin <- lm(total_sightings ~ t, data = ymeans)
expo <- lm(log(total_sightings) ~ t, data = ymeans)
plot(ymeans$Year, ymeans$total_sightings, pch = 16, col = "grey30",
     xlab = "year", ylab = "mean count per route")
lines(ymeans$Year, predict(lin), col = "grey45", lwd = 3)
lines(ymeans$Year, exp(predict(expo)), col = "red", lwd = 3)
legend("topright", lwd = 3, col = c("grey45", "red"), bty = "n", cex = 0.9,
       legend = c("linear, SS = 28.6", "exponential, SS = 28.1"))
```

Over 24 years, the data **cannot tell them apart**.

. . .

So choose on what they do **outside** the data: the linear model hits zero in
2041. We are extrapolating 20 years, so the choice matters.

::: {.notes}
Fit both to the real yearly means and the residual sums of squares are 28.6 and
28.1. That is a tie, and it is the honest outcome: 24 years of a gentle decline
is not enough curvature to distinguish a line from an exponential.

So the fit does not decide it, which is a useful thing for students to see. Two
other things do:

- **Mechanism.** Losing a constant fraction follows from births and deaths being
  proportional to abundance. Losing a constant number does not follow from
  anything, unless an outside process is removing a fixed amount.
- **Extrapolation.** We are about to simulate 20 years forward. The linear model
  predicts zero bobwhite in 2041 and negative numbers after that. The exponential
  predicts about 4.4 birds per route after 40 years.

The general lesson, and it is Bolker's: when two models fit equally well, pick
the one whose assumptions you believe, especially if you are going to ask it
questions outside the range of the data.
:::

## 2. What distribution for the counts? {.smaller}

Counts of birds on a route: whole numbers, no ceiling, and **clumped**, because
habitat varies from route to route.

| Candidate | Why not |
|---|---|
| Normal | counts are whole numbers and cannot be negative |
| Poisson | requires variance = mean |
| **Negative binomial** | counts, no ceiling, variance can exceed the mean |

. . .

Normal is out on sight. **Poisson makes a claim we can test.**

::: {.notes}
The elimination procedure from Lecture 12. Normal goes immediately: these are
whole numbers and cannot be negative.

Poisson is the interesting one, because it is the obvious choice for counts and
it stakes a claim: variance equals mean. The next slide checks it against the
real data instead of taking anyone's word for it.
:::

## Testing the Poisson claim {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
counts_real <- bobwhite$total_sightings

mean(counts_real)
var(counts_real)

mean(counts_real >= 40)                            # observed

ppois(39, lambda = mean(counts_real), lower.tail = FALSE)   # Poisson says
```
:::

| | observed | Poisson says |
|---|---|---|
| variance | [111]{.fragment fragment-index=1} | [11]{.fragment fragment-index=2} |
| P(count $\geq$ 40) | [0.024]{.fragment fragment-index=1} | [0.000000000007]{.fragment fragment-index=2} |

[A Poisson is **fixed once you know the mean**: its variance *is* the mean, and
`ppois()` needs nothing else. That is why it has no way to match these data.
The negative binomial has a second parameter, so it has a chance.]{.fragment fragment-index=3}

::: {.notes}
Four minutes on the code, then fill the table in with the arrow key, so each
number arrives after the room has produced it.

- **First press:** the observed column, from their own output.
- **Second press:** what a Poisson predicts, also on their screen.
- **Third press:** the sentence underneath.

Worth asking them to guess the Poisson number before the second press. The gap
between any guess and 7 x 10^-12 is the lesson.

The Poisson is not slightly wrong, it is wrong by ten orders of magnitude on the
thing that matters. It has one parameter and the data have already used it up on
the mean.

Do not show the negative binomial yet. It needs a second parameter, which is the
next slide, and then we come back and run the same test on it.

Read the last row out loud. About one route-year in forty has 40 or more
bobwhite. A Poisson with this mean says that happens once in 150 billion. The
negative binomial, with its clumping parameter estimated from these same data,
says one in forty-three.

That is a model check in the Lecture 13 sense: ask the candidate to predict
something, then look.

The predictions come from the p functions in Lecture 12's four-letter family.
`ppois(39, lambda, lower.tail = FALSE)` is on the slide for the Poisson column.
The negative binomial column is `pnbinom(39, mu = 10.8, size = 1.15,
lower.tail = FALSE)`, and the 1.15 is the clumping parameter from the next
slide, so it is worth coming back to this table after they have estimated it.

Nobody is fitting anything yet. The Poisson prediction needs no fitting at all,
because the mean determines everything about it, which is the point of the
sentence under the table.

One honest caveat about this file: it only contains rows for routes where the
species was seen, so there are no true zeros in it. Our simulation will generate
some, which makes it slightly pessimistic.
:::

## 3. The parameters come from the data {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
mu0 <- mean(bobwhite$total_sightings)
v <- var(bobwhite$total_sightings)

size <- mu0^2 / (v - mu0)

round(c(mean = mu0, variance = v, size = size), 2)

mu0 + mu0^2 / size          # the variance this negative binomial implies
```
:::

| Parameter | Value | Where it came from |
|---|---|---|
| $\mu_0$, starting mean | 10.8 | the data |
| $k$, clumping | 1.15 | the data, by matching the variance |
| $d$, annual decline | 0.03 | the published trend, **the effect we want to detect** |

::: {.notes}
Method of moments: set the distribution's mean and variance equal to the data's,
then solve for size.

The last line is the check that it worked. A negative binomial with this mean and
this size has variance mu + mu^2/k, which comes back as 111, the variance we
started from. That is not a coincidence and it is not evidence either: we chose
size to make it true. The real test is the next slide.

The table is worth pausing on, because the three parameters have different
statuses. Two are estimates from survey data. The third, d, is a choice: it is
the effect we want the program to be able to detect, taken from the published
trend. Nothing in the data forced it, and if we cared about a 1% decline we would
need a very different program, which we check later.

That distinction is Tuesday's "one number nobody can give you".
:::

## Does the negative binomial pass the same test? {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

The variance matches, but we **made** it match. Try something we did not fit:

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
pnbinom(39, mu = mu0, size = size, lower.tail = FALSE)
```
:::

| | observed | Poisson said | Negative binomial says |
|---|---|---|---|
| variance | 111 | 11 | 111, by construction |
| P(count $\geq$ 40) | 0.024 | 0.000000000007 | [0.023]{.fragment fragment-index=1} |

[Nothing in the fitting used the tail. **That** is a real test, and it
passes.]{.fragment fragment-index=2}

::: {.notes}
Three minutes, and the payoff for having estimated `size` on the last slide.

Ask them to predict before the reveal: the Poisson was out by a factor of three
billion on this row, so what will the negative binomial do?

The answer is 0.023 against 0.024 observed. Nothing in the fitting used how often
counts exceed 40, so this is a genuine prediction rather than a restatement of
the input, which is what makes it worth something.

This is the Lecture 13 idea stated carefully: a model check is only informative
about the parts of the data you did not use to fit it.

So: Poisson rejected, negative binomial survives, and we have the numbers we
need.
:::

## The model, in one place {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Math**

Expected count in year $t$:

$$\mu_t = \mu_0\,(1 - d)^{\,t}$$

Counts around it:

$$y_t \sim \text{NegBinomial}(\mu_t,\; k)$$

with $\mu_0 = 10.8$, $d = 0.03$, $k = 1.15$.
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
**R**

```{r}
#| eval: false
mu <- mu0 * (1 - d)^year

counts <- rnbinom(n = length(year),
                  mu = mu,
                  size = k)
```

**How we will analyze it**

```{r}
#| eval: false
lm(log(counts + 1) ~ year)
```
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
The three decisions assembled. Chapter 3 gives the curve, chapter 4 gives the
scatter, and the data gave the numbers.

Why log the counts for fitting: a constant fractional decline is a straight line
on a log scale, so a test of the slope is a test for decline. The +1 is there
because these counts include zeros and log(0) is undefined.

That transform is a compromise and it is worth admitting: it biases the estimated
rate slightly toward zero. Chapter 9 fits this properly with a GLM. Nothing today
turns on the difference.

Next three slides build this up one line at a time.
:::

## What we are actually choosing {.smaller}

The model is settled. What is **not** settled is the survey itself.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="48%"}
**Fixed:** the budget

$$\text{routes} \times \text{years} = 400$$

One route surveyed in one year is one visit, and the agency can pay for 400 of
them.
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
**Yours to choose:** the allocation

- Many routes, few years? **Space**
- Few routes, many years? **Time**
:::

::::

. . .

The model says what the birds do. The **design** says where and when you look.

::: {.notes}
Bring them back to the actual decision before the mechanics start, because the
last six slides were about bobwhite and distributions and it is easy to lose the
thread.

Say the separation plainly, because it is the idea the whole lecture turns on:
mu0, k and d describe the population and are not ours to change. Routes and years
describe the survey and are entirely ours to change. Power depends on both.

The constraint is what makes it interesting. Without a budget the answer is
always "collect more data", which is true and useless.

Next three slides build one design, 40 routes for 10 years, and then they vote
on how to spend the 400 visits.
:::

## Step 1: the expected counts {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
mu0 <- 10.8
k <- 1.15
d <- 0.03

n_routes <- 40
n_years <- 10

year <- rep(0:(n_years - 1), each = n_routes)

mu <- mu0 * (1 - d)^year

plot(year, mu, ylim = c(0, 12))
```
:::

400 route-visits: 40 routes, each surveyed for 10 years. No randomness yet.

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. This is the deterministic part on its own, which is the same way
Lecture 13 started.

Point at the year vector: `rep(0:9, each = 40)` gives 40 routes in year 0, 40 in
year 1, and so on, which is what a monitoring program actually produces.

The plot is a smooth curve because every route in a given year has the same
expectation. All the differences between routes are about to come from the
distribution.
:::

## Step 2: add the noise {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
counts <- rnbinom(n = length(year), mu = mu, size = k)

plot(jitter(year), counts)
points(year, mu, col = "red", pch = 16)
```
:::

That is **one monitoring program**: 400 counts, and the truth in red.

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. Have them run it several times before moving on.

jitter() spreads the points horizontally so overlapping counts are visible. Worth
naming, they will want it again.

The reaction to aim for: the red curve is a gentle decline and the black points
look like a cloud. If you did not know the answer, you would not see it by eye.
That is the whole problem, and it is why we need the test rather than a look.
:::

## Step 3: analyze it like real data {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
m <- lm(log(counts + 1) ~ year)

summary(m)$coefficients["year", ]
```
:::

Two things to read:

- Is the **slope** negative, as it should be?
- Is **`Pr(>|t|)`** below 0.05?

::: {.notes}
Five minutes, and the step students skip when left alone: analyze the fake data
exactly as you would analyze the real thing.

The true slope is log(0.97) = -0.031, so a correct answer is a small negative
number. Someone will get a positive one, which is the point of the next slide.

Have a few people call out their p-value. The spread across the room is the
lesson, and it is free.
:::

## Four programs, four answers

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.3
#| fig-width: 9
set.seed(11)
par(mfrow = c(1, 4), mar = c(3.2, 3.2, 2.2, 0.5), mgp = c(1.9, 0.6, 0))
yrv <- rep(0:9, each = 40)
for (i in 1:4) {
  cnt <- rnbinom(length(yrv), mu = 10.8 * 0.97^yrv, size = 1.15)
  mm <- lm(log(cnt + 1) ~ yrv)
  p <- summary(mm)$coefficients["yrv", "Pr(>|t|)"]
  plot(jitter(yrv, 0.6), log(cnt + 1), pch = 16, cex = 0.5,
       col = rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.35), xlab = "year", ylab = "log(count + 1)",
       main = sprintf("p = %.3f", p),
       col.main = if (p < 0.05) "firebrick" else "grey30")
  abline(mm, col = if (p < 0.05) "firebrick" else "grey40", lwd = 3)
}
```

Same truth, same design, four runs. **One detected it. Two slope the wrong way.**

::: {.notes}
This is the slide to slow down on.

Every one of these programs ran for 10 years on 40 routes while the population
really was declining at 3% a year. One of them found it. Two of them came back
suggesting an increase.

That is not a mistake by the analyst, it is what 400 noisy counts can support.
Anyone who has wondered why monitoring programs disagree has their answer.

It also makes the next step obvious: you cannot judge a design from one run.
:::

## One study is not enough

Power is the **proportion** of programs that find the decline. So run many:

```{r}
#| eval: false
nsim <- 500
found <- numeric(nsim)

for (i in 1:nsim) {

  counts <- rnbinom(n = length(year), mu = mu, size = k)
  m <- lm(log(counts + 1) ~ year)

  found[i] <- summary(m)$coefficients["year", "Pr(>|t|)"] < 0.05

}

mean(found)      # this is the power
```

::: {.notes}
The for loop from Lecture 7, now with a reason to exist.

Three parts worth naming: create an empty vector, fill one slot per pass,
summarize at the end. That is the shape of every simulation loop, and it is what
the midterm skeleton does.

mean() of TRUE and FALSE gives the proportion that are TRUE, which is worth
pointing out.
:::

## Reading the output {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.0
#| fig-width: 6.8
set.seed(21)
yrv <- rep(0:9, each = 40)
res <- replicate(500, {
  cnt <- rnbinom(length(yrv), mu = 10.8 * 0.97^yrv, size = 1.15)
  mm <- lm(log(cnt + 1) ~ yrv)
  c(coef(mm)["yrv"], summary(mm)$coefficients["yrv", "Pr(>|t|)"])
})
pw <- mean(res[2, ] < 0.05 & res[1, ] < 0)
hist(res[1, ], breaks = 30, col = "grey85", main = "",
     xlab = "estimated slope of log count on year")
abline(v = log(0.97), col = "red", lwd = 3)
```

500 programs. True slope in red. **About a third** landed far enough from zero to
be called significant.

::: {.notes}
The loop gives one number, the power, but the distribution behind it is worth
seeing. It is the same figure as Tuesday's 10-sites-against-40 slide, on a real
problem.

Three things to point at:

- The estimates are centered near the truth, so the method is roughly unbiased,
  though the log(x+1) transform pulls it slightly toward zero.
- A noticeable share are on the wrong side of zero, which is the two wrong-way
  panels from the last slide.
- Power is just the proportion of this histogram that clears the significance
  threshold.

If anyone asks why not report the mean estimate instead: that is a better
question than it sounds, and precision, the width of this histogram, is often
more useful than power.
:::

## Your turn: compute the power of one design {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
year <- rep(0:9, each = 40)       # 40 routes, 10 years
mu <- 10.8 * (1 - 0.03)^year

found <- numeric(500)

for (i in 1:500) {
  counts <- rnbinom(n = length(year), mu = mu, size = 1.15)
  m <- lm(log(counts + 1) ~ year)
  found[i] <- summary(m)$coefficients["year", "Pr(>|t|)"] < 0.05
}

mean(found)
```
:::

400 route-visits. **Would you fund this program?**

::: {.notes}
Six minutes. Everyone should land near 0.36, give or take sampling noise.

Then ask the question and let them sit with it. A program that costs 400
route-visits and has a one in three chance of detecting a decline that is really
happening is not a good use of public money, and most of them will feel that
before they can say why.

Nobody should change the design yet. That is the next slide, and the vote has to
come first.
:::

## The decision {.center}

## Same budget, four designs {background-color="#f0f4f8"}

All cost **400 route-visits**. Which would you fund?

| | Routes | Years |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | 200 | 2 |
| **B** | 80 | 5 |
| **C** | 40 | 10 |
| **D** | 20 | 20 |

**Commit to one before we run it.** Hands up for each.

::: {.notes}
The commitment matters, so take the vote properly: hands up for A, B, C, D, and
write the counts on the board. A show of hands they have to hold makes the
reveal land in a way that a rhetorical question does not.

Ask one person from each camp to say why in a sentence. Common reasoning: more
routes means a bigger sample and better averages, which is the intuition the
next slide overturns.

Expect most votes on B and C. In my experience almost nobody picks D, which is
the right answer.
:::

## The answer

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-width: 7
set.seed(14)
designs <- data.frame(label = c("A\n200 x 2", "B\n80 x 5", "C\n40 x 10", "D\n20 x 20"),
                      routes = c(200, 80, 40, 20), years = c(2, 5, 10, 20))
designs$power <- mapply(power_design, designs$routes, designs$years)
par(mar = c(3.6, 3.6, 0.6, 0.6), mgp = c(2.3, 0.7, 0))
bp <- barplot(designs$power, names.arg = designs$label, ylim = c(0, 1),
              col = c("grey80", "grey80", "grey80", "firebrick"),
              ylab = "power to detect the decline", xlab = "")
text(bp, designs$power + 0.05, sprintf("%.2f", designs$power), cex = 1.1)
abline(h = 0.8, lty = 2, col = "blue")
text(bp[1], 0.85, "0.8: the usual target", col = "blue", cex = 0.95, adj = 0)
```

Same cost. **5% against 90%.**

::: {.notes}
The dashed blue line is power = 0.8, the conventional target: a design that
would catch a real decline four times out of five. Only D clears it.

Worth saying that 0.8 is a convention, not a law. It comes from Cohen, who
proposed it as a reasonable default, and it amounts to accepting a one in five
chance of missing a real effect. If missing the decline would be expensive, 0.8
is not high enough.

Let the numbers sit before explaining. The gap between A and D is the single most
useful thing in this lecture: identical budget, and one design is almost useless
while the other is good.

If the room voted mostly B and C, say so, and say that this is the normal
intuition and it is wrong. That is worth more than being told the rule.
:::

## Why years beat routes

A trend is a **slope over time**. Slopes are estimated from the **spread of the
x values**.

. . .

- Adding **years** stretches the x axis: 2 years of change against 20 years of
  change
- Adding **routes** only averages the noise at the years you already have

. . .

With 2 years, the population has declined about 6% in total. There is almost
nothing to detect.

::: {.notes}
This is the mechanism, and it generalizes well beyond birds. Any time the
question is about a rate of change, the range of the predictor is what buys you
precision, and replication at a few values of the predictor is a poor substitute.

Connect to Lecture 13: the "break it" exercise showed that detecting a slope
depends on the ratio of signal to noise. Here extending the time series grows the
signal, while adding routes only shrinks the noise a little.

The caution worth adding: this is specific to estimating a trend. If the question
were "how many bobwhite are there this year", routes would be exactly what you
want and years would be useless.
:::

## How long before you would know?

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-width: 6.6
set.seed(15)
years <- c(3, 5, 8, 10, 15, 20, 25)
pw <- sapply(years, function(y) power_design(30, y))
par(mar = c(3.6, 3.6, 0.6, 0.6), mgp = c(2.3, 0.7, 0))
plot(years, pw, type = "b", pch = 16, lwd = 2, ylim = c(0, 1),
     xlab = "years of monitoring (30 routes)", ylab = "power")
abline(h = 0.8, lty = 2, col = "blue")
text(3, 0.85, "0.8: the usual target", col = "blue", cex = 0.95, adj = 0)
```

At 30 routes, a 3% decline needs about **18 years** before you would
reliably catch it.

::: {.notes}
The sobering slide, and the honest one. Power is 0.05 at 3 years, 0.24 at 10,
and 0.68 at 15, so a short program aimed at a gradual decline is mostly wasted
money.

This is also why the BBS matters: it has been running since 1966, which is why
anybody knows bobwhite are declining at all.

Ask what they would tell the agency if the agency can only commit to 5 years. A
good answer: either accept that you are measuring something else, such as current
abundance, or find a more sensitive response than counts.
:::

## Your turn: what if the decline is worse? {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
year <- rep(0:9, each = 40)   # 40 routes, 10 years

decline <- 0.03               # try 0.01, 0.05, 0.10

found <- numeric(500)
for (i in 1:500) {
  counts <- rnbinom(length(year), mu = 10.8 * (1 - decline)^year, size = 1.15)
  m <- lm(log(counts + 1) ~ year)
  found[i] <- summary(m)$coefficients["year", "Pr(>|t|)"] < 0.05
}
mean(found)
```
:::

Which is easier to detect, a slow decline or a fast one?

::: {.notes}
Six minutes. A 10% annual decline is easy to catch even in 10 years; a 1% decline
is nearly hopeless at this design.

The lesson to name: power is not a property of a study, it is a property of a
study **and** an effect size. "Is this study well powered" has no answer until
somebody says how big an effect matters.

Which is the point from Tuesday: the smallest effect worth detecting is a
judgment call, and it belongs in the methods section.
:::

## Three honest warnings {.smaller}

**Power is not a p-value.** It is computed before you have data, from assumptions
you chose.

. . .

**Post-hoc power is useless.** Computing power from your observed effect after a
non-significant result tells you nothing new.

. . .

**A significant result from an underpowered study is not reassuring.** When power
is low, the effects that do reach significance are the overestimates.

::: {.notes}
The third one is the least known and the most important. With power at 0.2, a
study only reaches significance when the noise happens to help, so published
effects from small studies are systematically too big. That is a large part of
why replications come back smaller.

This connects to Lecture 13's figure: at a small sample size the slope estimates
were spread from about -0.6 to 2.9, and the significant ones are the far right of
that distribution.

Post-hoc power is worth naming because reviewers still ask for it.
:::

## Now one of your own {.center}

::: {.notes}
The rest of the period. Same job as the bobwhite, different system, and much less
told to them.

They work in pairs or small groups; you circulate. The slides give the five
decisions and a skeleton with blanks, so nobody is stuck staring at an empty
script, but every function name is theirs to recall.
:::

## Do protected reefs hold more fish? {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

NOAA surveys reefs across the Florida Keys, inside and outside protected areas,
and records the fish seen on each survey.

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
reef <- read.csv("https://github.com/bmaitner/biometry_course/raw/refs/heads/main/data/Reef_fish/NCRMP_reef_fish_surveys.csv")

reef$protected <- ifelse(reef$PROT == 0, "no", "yes")

# 8 of the 8560 surveys recorded no fish at all. log(0) is -Inf, which would
# wreck every summary below, so set them aside.
reef <- reef[reef$total_abundance > 0, ]
```
:::

**The question:** a manager wants to know whether protection works. How many
surveys per group would it take to find out?

::: {.notes}
Same job as the bobwhite, different in two ways that matter: the comparison is
between two groups rather than across time, and the response is not a count.

`total_abundance` is fish per survey, standardized for effort, so it is a
positive continuous number rather than a whole one. That changes the
distribution, and figuring that out is part of the exercise.

PROT has three codes; 0 is unprotected and 1 and 2 are two kinds of protection,
which is why they get collapsed.

The zeros line is given to them because it is a data-cleaning trap rather than
the skill being practised, and last year it stopped people before they got to
the statistics. It is still worth thirty seconds out loud: 8 surveys in 8560 saw
no fish, log(0) is -Inf, and one -Inf turns a mean into -Inf. Dropping 0.1% of
the data is defensible here, and the rule is that you say you did it rather than
quietly filtering.

Worth adding that if they had chosen a gamma instead of a lognormal, zeros would
break that too, for the same reason.
:::

## 1. What is the deterministic part? {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

For the bobwhite it was a curve through time. Here there is **no time axis**:
just two groups with different expected abundance.

So the deterministic part is a pair of means. Your decision:

- Describe the effect as a **difference** (protected minus unprotected), or
- Describe it as a **ratio** (protected divided by unprotected)?

Plot it both ways before you choose:

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
unprot <- reef$total_abundance[reef$protected == "no"]
prot   <- reef$total_abundance[reef$protected == "yes"]

hist(unprot)                 # raw scale
hist(log(unprot))            # log scale: which looks symmetric?

____                         # now do the same for prot
```
:::

::: {.notes}
A short one, but the decision is real and it sets up everything after it.

What they should find: abundance is positive and right skewed, so a difference
of means is awkward and a ratio is natural. "Protected reefs hold 50% more fish"
travels better than "73 more fish per survey", and it does not depend on where
you sampled.

A ratio on the raw scale is a difference on the log scale, which is the hinge
between this decision and the next two.

Do not tell them this. Ask what a histogram of each group looks like.
:::

## 2. Which distribution? {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

Fish per survey is positive, continuous, and right skewed.

| Candidate | Rule it in or out |
|---|---|
| Normal | [allows negatives, and the data are skewed]{.fragment fragment-index=1} |
| Poisson | [these are not whole numbers, see below]{.fragment fragment-index=2} |
| Lognormal or gamma | [positive, continuous, right skewed: both plausible]{.fragment fragment-index=3} |

**"Abundance" sounds like a count. Check before you assume:**

```{r}
#| eval: false
head(sort(unique(reef$total_abundance)))     # 0.0  0.5  1.0  1.5  2.0  2.5
```

Then **check it the way we checked the Poisson**: make it predict something.

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
mean(unprot > 500)           # observed: how often is a survey this rich?

____(500, meanlog = ____, sdlog = ____, lower.tail = FALSE)
#  ^ the p-function for your chosen distribution
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Let them fill the right column before revealing it. Two of the three are quick.

The Poisson row needs explaining, because "abundance" sounds like a count and
students reasonably reach for a count distribution. These numbers are not raw
tallies: the monitoring program reports fish per standard survey area, averaged
over the replicate observations that make up a survey, so halves and decimals
appear. About half the values in the column are not whole numbers.

The habit worth teaching is the one line on the slide: before choosing a
discrete distribution, look at whether the values are actually whole numbers.
Counting *things* does not guarantee the recorded variable is an integer, and
densities, rates and averages all look like counts in a column name.

The last row is the interesting one, because two candidates survive and the data
will not strongly separate them. That is normal, and Lecture 12's advice applies:
pick one, say why, and note that the other was defensible.

A good check for lognormal: if abundance is lognormal then log(abundance) is
normal, so a histogram of the logs should look symmetric. That is one line and
they have done it before, on bird mass.

A stronger check, if anyone wants it: compare the observed proportion above some
high value against what their fitted distribution predicts, exactly as we did
with P(count >= 40).
:::

## 3. The parameters {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

Estimate these from the data yourselves, on the scale your distribution works
on:

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
meanlog_unprot <- ____(log(unprot))     # centre, on the log scale
sdlog_unprot   <- ____(log(unprot))     # spread, on the log scale

meanlog_prot <- ____
sdlog_prot   <- ____
```
:::

Two questions worth asking of your answers:

- Is the **spread** similar in the two groups? Does that simplify the simulation?
- What **ratio** do the two centres imply?

::: {.notes}
They have estimated parameters twice today, so this is deliberately bare.

If they chose lognormal, the parameters are the mean and sd of the logged
values, which is what rlnorm wants. Anyone who hands rlnorm the raw mean will
get absurd numbers, and that is a useful mistake to make here rather than on the
midterm.

The two questions matter. The spreads come out nearly identical, which justifies
simulating both groups with one spread. The ratio of centres is the effect size
actually present in these reefs, and it is smaller than people expect.
:::

## 4. What are you choosing? {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="48%"}
**Fixed:** survey effort. Say the agency can fund **120 surveys** in total.
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
**Yours to choose:**

- How many go in each group
- Which effect size you want to be able to detect
:::

::::

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
n_per_group <- 60        # 120 surveys, split evenly. Your call.
effect <- 1.5            # the ratio you want to be able to detect. Also your call.
```
:::

The second one is not in the data. **You have to decide what difference would
matter** before power means anything.

::: {.notes}
The same separation as the bobwhite: the reef biology is not ours to change, the
survey design is.

Unlike the bobwhite there are two things to choose here, and the second is the
one from Tuesday that no dataset can give them. A 50% difference in fish
abundance would change management. A 5% difference probably would not.

If anyone asks what to use: have them run both the difference they care about
and the difference actually present in the data, and compare. That contrast is
the point of the last slide.
:::

## 5. Simulate, analyze, repeat {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
# one study: draw each group from your distribution
sim_unprot <- ____(n_per_group, meanlog = meanlog_unprot, sdlog = sdlog_unprot)

# adding log(effect) on the log scale multiplies by effect on the fish scale
sim_prot   <- ____(n_per_group, meanlog = meanlog_unprot + log(effect),
                   sdlog = sdlog_unprot)

# analyze it the way you would analyze the real surveys
____                                      # compare the two groups, get a p-value

# many studies
found <- numeric(500)
for (i in 1:500) {
  ____                                    # the two draws again
  found[i] <- ____ < 0.05                 # did this study find the difference?
}
mean(found)                               # the power
```
:::

Why **add** when the effect is a ratio? Because
$e^{\,m + \log 1.5} = 1.5\,e^{\,m}$: a shift on the log scale is a
multiplication on the original scale.

Then vary `n_per_group`, and find where power reaches **0.8**.

::: {.notes}
No function names, on purpose. Everything they need they have used: the r
functions from Lecture 12, the loop from today, and a two-group comparison.

The step people get wrong is the analysis: with a skewed response, comparing the
groups on the log scale is the sensible choice, and it is also the scale they
simulated on.

Spend a moment on the adding-versus-multiplying point, because students who are
shaky on logs will read `meanlog + log(effect)` as adding fish. Say it in
numbers: meanlog is 4.90, log(1.5) is 0.41, so the protected group has meanlog
5.31, and exp(5.31) is 201 against exp(4.90) = 134. That is 1.5 times as many
fish, produced by an addition.

The same identity is why the bobwhite decline was a straight line on the log
scale: multiplying by 0.97 each year is subtracting 0.03 each year in logs.

Circulate. The question to ask anyone who is stuck is "what would you do if these
were the real data?", because the answer to that is the answer here.

Anyone who finishes early: what if effort is split unevenly, say 30 and 90?
:::

## If something breaks {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

Three things that trip people up here:

- **`-Inf` or `NaN` in your summaries.** Something got logged that should not
  have been, or a zero slipped through.
- **Simulated numbers in the millions.** `rlnorm()` wants the mean and sd *of the
  logs*, not of the raw abundances. Check that your `meanlog` is around 5, not
  around 150.
- **Power of 1.00 at every sample size.** Your two groups are probably further
  apart than you meant. Print the ratio you are simulating.

::: {.notes}
Put this up once most groups are simulating, or point individuals at it. It is
deliberately a list of symptoms rather than fixes, so they still do the
diagnosis.

The second one is the big one and it is worth repeating out loud: meanlog near 5
means a median around 150 fish, because exp(5) is about 150. Anyone whose
simulated surveys have ten thousand fish has handed rlnorm a raw mean.

The third catches people who set effect to 15 rather than 1.5.
:::

## Check yourself {.smaller}

Distribution: **lognormal** works well here, gamma is defensible.
What the real data say:

| | unprotected | protected |
|---|---|---|
| median fish per survey | [139]{.fragment fragment-index=1} | [171]{.fragment fragment-index=1} |
| sd of log abundance | [0.90]{.fragment fragment-index=2} | [0.91]{.fragment fragment-index=2} |

. . .

Power to detect a **50% difference**: about [0.27 at n = 20, 0.69 at n = 60,
0.88 at n = 100]{.fragment fragment-index=4}

Power to detect the **23% difference actually observed**: about [0.23 at
n = 60, and still only 0.65 at n = 200]{.fragment fragment-index=5}

::: {.notes}
Reveal these one at a time as groups get there, or at the end if you are short of
time.

The last line is the honest and uncomfortable result, and it is the reason this
exercise is worth doing. The difference these reefs actually show is about 23%,
and reaching 0.8 for an effect that size takes roughly 400 surveys per group. A
manager with 120 surveys to spend cannot answer this question, and knowing that
in advance is worth more than running it and getting a shrug.

The 60 per group they were given lands at about 0.69 for a 50% difference and
0.23 for the real one.

Expect their numbers to differ in the second decimal. 500 simulations gives a
power estimate good to about plus or minus 0.02, which is worth saying: the
simulation has sampling error too.

Two things worth drawing out if there is time:

- The sd of log abundance is nearly identical in the two groups, which is a tidy
  justification for simulating both with the same spread.
- Protection may well work and still be undetectable at this sample size. Failing
  to detect is not evidence of no effect, which is the third warning from
  earlier, met in the wild.
:::

## Additional practice

On your own, extend the bobwhite simulation:

- What if routes differ in quality, some good and some poor?
- What if you survey each route twice a year?
- What if the agency can afford 800 visits?

::: {.notes}
Take-home, not class time. Each one is a small change to code they already have.

The first is the groups idea from Tuesday applied here: draw each route's own
mean, then counts within it. It is also the most realistic of the three, because
real routes do differ.

The second is worth attempting because the answer surprises people: two visits a
year helps far less than one extra year does, for the same reason years beat
routes.

Anyone who wants more should put the time into the midterm instead.
:::
